title: Voice Agent Engineering — Nik Caryotakis, SuperDial
talk_summary: SuperDial describes building reliable voice agents by owning an OpenAI-compatible routing layer, self-hosting orchestration/observability, and treating the last mile—pronunciation, fallbacks, and end-to-end tests—as the real work. The transferable lesson is to invest in routing/fallbacks, per-step observability, and realistic test harnesses rather than the demo model.

takeaways.what_they_do: They own an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and route behind it to different models, including latency-sensitive ones, via TensorZero.
takeaways.evidence_quote: behind our open a endpoint we can kind of route to different models

takeaways.what_they_do: The voice bot tries the call; if it needs a human or fails after a set number of attempts, it escalates to a fallback team.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if our voice spot needs to bring in a human to complete the call

takeaways.what_they_do: They self-host Langfuse and run anomaly detection, evals, and datasets on production calls.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we do like anomaly detection evals and data sets

takeaways.what_they_do: They test the bot against a fake phone number playing an MP3, simulated phone trees, and bot-to-bot conversations.
takeaways.evidence_quote: create a kind of fake phone number that just plays an MP3

takeaways.what_they_do: Use conversation-design table reads: one person plays the bot, one the user, and reading the transcript aloud exposes gaps.
takeaways.evidence_quote: have one person pretend to be the bot and the other person to pretend to be a user

takeaways.what_they_do: They track latency everywhere, especially time-to-first-byte for each processor in the pipeline.
takeaways.evidence_quote: track latency everywhere time to First Bite for each of your little processors
